chapters.title: PESTLE Analysis
chapters.description: External political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental influences.

questions.stem: [1] A government announces a sustained programme of higher public spending and also signals that it will maintain strict control of public finances. Which PESTLE category is most directly concerned with these developments?
questions.explanation: Government spending and fiscal policy are classified as Political in this PESTLE teaching framework; they also have economic effects.
questions.source: Original question 1; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [2] An SME completes a PESTLE analysis and concludes that it has a strong internal capability to exploit a new market. Why should this conclusion not be treated as a PESTLE finding by itself?

options.text: PESTLE focuses on the external environment and does not assess internal strengths, weaknesses or capabilities
PESTLE is designed only to analyse financial statements
PESTLE cannot be used for strategic planning

questions.explanation: PESTLE examines external conditions. Internal capabilities belong in an internal analysis such as SWOT.
questions.source: Original question 2; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [3] A bakery’s customers have experienced rising prices for many goods. The bakery is concerned that, even where nominal household incomes rise, customers may have less purchasing power. Which PESTLE factor is most relevant?
questions.explanation: Real income measures purchasing power after allowing for changes in prices.
questions.source: Original question 3; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [4] An Irish business is considering selling more products in the UK. The euro falls in value relative to sterling. What is the most direct effect of this currency depreciation on goods imported from the UK into Ireland?
questions.explanation: A weaker euro buys fewer pounds, raising the euro cost of UK imports, other things equal.
questions.source: Original question 4; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [5] An SME bakery finds that changes in the age structure of the population are altering demand for different types of baked goods. Which PESTLE category does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Age structure and demographics are Social factors.
questions.source: Original question 5; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [6] A bakery introduces automated production equipment and robotics to speed up its production process and reduce costs. Which PESTLE category best captures this development?
questions.explanation: Automation and robotics fall under Technological factors.
questions.source: Original question 6; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [7] A company must change how it stores and processes customers’ personal information because of the GDPR. Which PESTLE category should this issue be placed under?
questions.explanation: Data-protection obligations are Legal factors.
questions.source: Original question 7; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [8] A business is assessing how climate change, carbon-reduction pressures and the transition to lower-emission operations could affect its costs and long-term plans. Which PESTLE category is most directly relevant?
questions.explanation: Climate and sustainability pressures are Environmental factors.
questions.source: Original question 8; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [9] A manager uses PESTLE analysis to identify an emerging external threat before it has a serious effect on the business. Which advantage of PESTLE is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: PESTLE can identify external risks early.
questions.source: Original question 9; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [10] A PESTLE exercise produces such a long list of possible external developments that managers cannot decide which issues to act on. Which disadvantage of PESTLE does this best illustrate?
questions.explanation: Too many findings without priorities can produce analysis paralysis.
questions.source: Original question 10; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [11] An Irish SME bakery is considering expanding into the UK. The management team is particularly concerned that changes in the euro–sterling exchange rate could alter the cost of ingredients and other imported inputs. Which PESTLE factor should it examine most directly?
questions.explanation: Exchange-rate movements are Economic factors.
questions.source: Original question 11; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [12] An SME wants to improve its green credentials and asks managers to use PESTLE analysis. The team produces a long list of climate, carbon-pricing and sustainability issues but cannot decide which ones should influence its strategy. Which disadvantage of PESTLE is most clearly illustrated?
questions.explanation: An unprioritised list prevents decisions: analysis paralysis.
questions.source: Original question 12; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [13] An Irish bakery considering UK expansion is researching whether demand in the UK may differ from demand in Ireland because of differences in customer tastes, culture and demographic patterns. Which PESTLE category is most relevant?
questions.explanation: Culture, preferences and demographics are Social factors.
questions.source: Original question 13; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [14] A pharmaceutical company is considering moving some operations from Cork to Poland. Before making the investment, managers want to assess how regulation and employment-law requirements, including statutory minimum-wage rules, could affect the operation. Which PESTLE category is this?
questions.explanation: Regulation, employment law and statutory wage requirements are Legal factors.
questions.source: Original question 14; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [15] A pharmaceutical company assessing a new international supply chain is also assessing the risks associated with political stability, geopolitical developments and trade policy in the countries connected to its new supply chain. Which PESTLE category captures these issues?
questions.explanation: Political stability, geopolitical risk and trade policy are Political factors.
questions.source: Original question 15; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [16] An IT company is considering a major new investment in Ireland. Its managers want to understand how rapid developments in AI, digitalisation, payment systems and cybersecurity could affect the competitiveness of the investment. Which PESTLE category should they focus on?
questions.explanation: AI, digitalisation and cybersecurity are Technological factors.
questions.source: Original question 16; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [17] An IT company is deciding whether to increase its investment in Ireland. One part of its external-environment assessment considers government spending, corporate and personal tax, fiscal risks and political stability. Which PESTLE category does this describe?
questions.explanation: Tax policy, government spending and political stability are Political in the lecture framework.
questions.source: Original question 17; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [18] An indigenous small IT company is considering expanding its product range. The owners believe that technological innovation could allow it to develop new products and increase the added value offered to customers. Which PESTLE category is most directly relevant to this external opportunity?
questions.explanation: Technological innovation can create external product-development opportunities.
questions.source: Original question 18; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [19] An SME agri-business is considering moving manufacturing to China. Its board wants to assess the possible impact of tariffs, trade policy and geopolitical risk on the proposed move. Which PESTLE category should be used?
questions.explanation: Tariffs, trade policy and geopolitical risk are Political factors.
questions.source: Original question 19; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [20] An agri-business considering moving manufacturing to China is also considering how access to raw materials and longer-term sustainability issues could affect the proposed manufacturing strategy. Which PESTLE category is most directly relevant?
questions.explanation: Natural-resource availability and sustainability are Environmental factors.
questions.source: Original question 20; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis

questions.stem: [Q1] A Cork medical-device exporter faces a new EU product-certification rule and a simultaneous fall in sterling. Which analysis best separates the two developments?

options.text: Certification is a legal factor; sterling depreciation is an economic factor that may reduce euro receipts from UK sales.
Certification is technological; sterling depreciation necessarily increases euro receipts.
Certification is social; exchange-rate changes cannot affect competitiveness.
Both are political factors, because governments influence each.

questions.explanation: Product-certification obligations are legal. Sterling depreciation can lower the euro value of sterling receipts, other things equal.
questions.source: Original question Q1; Lecture #1 — PESTLE Analysis; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

chapters.title: Goals of the Firm
chapters.description: Shareholder wealth, required returns, present value, investment decisions and basic profit relationships.

questions.stem: [21] Which statement best defines shareholder wealth?

options.text: The firm's total accounting profit in the current year
The present value of expected future cash returns to equity owners
The total value of the firm's outstanding bonds
The value of the firm's physical assets before liabilities

questions.explanation: Shareholder wealth concerns the value of expected future returns to equity owners.
questions.source: Original question 21; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [22] Why is shareholder wealth maximisation broader than simple profit maximisation?

options.text: It ignores risk but includes tax
It focuses only on the largest annual profit
It accounts for the timing and risk of expected future returns
It treats all stakeholders as equity owners

questions.explanation: Timing and risk matter as well as the amount of returns.
questions.source: Original question 22; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [23] Which option is not one of the three reasons given in Lecture #2 for discounting future money?
questions.explanation: Market share is not itself a reason to discount money.
questions.source: Original question 23; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [24] An investor requires a higher return from an oil-exploration project than from a safe deposit. Which concept best explains the difference?
questions.explanation: Additional investment risk can require a risk premium.
questions.source: Original question 24; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [25] Which formula correctly calculates the present value of a single future sum?
questions.explanation:
PV = FV / (1+r)^n

Divide the future sum by its compound discount factor.
questions.source: Original question 25; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [26] What is the approximate present value of €110 received in one year when the discount rate is 10%?
questions.source: Original question 26; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [27] Holding the future cash flow and time period constant, what happens when the discount rate rises?

options.text: Present value becomes equal to future value

questions.explanation: A larger discount denominator lowers present value for an unchanged positive cash flow.
questions.source: Original question 27; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [28] A share is expected to return €5, €6 and €7 at the ends of Years 1–3, respectively. The discount rate is 10%. What was their approximate total present value per share?
questions.explanation: €5/1.10 = €4.545455; €6/1.10² = €4.958678; €7/1.10³ = €5.259204. Add before rounding: €14.763336 ≈ €14.76. The earlier €14.77 used rounded intermediate values.
questions.source: Original question 28; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [29] Which approach is most appropriate when calculating the present value of several annual cash flows?

options.text: Add the undiscounted cash flows and discount the total once using Year 1
Discount each cash flow for its own time period and then add the present values
Use the risk-free rate even when a required return is supplied
Round every intermediate step to the nearest whole euro

questions.explanation: Discount each cash flow for the time until it is received, then sum.
questions.source: Original question 29; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [30] What does a positive NPV indicate?

options.text: The project fails to recover its initial cost in present-value terms
The project exactly earns the required return
The project adds value after allowing for the required return
The project's accounting profit must be zero

questions.explanation: Positive NPV means value is added above the required return.
questions.source: Original question 30; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [31] A project has an NPV of −€4,500. What decision follows from the standard NPV rule?

options.text: Accept because all cash inflows are positive
Accept because the initial investment is already paid
Reject because the project destroys value relative to the required return

questions.explanation: Negative NPV fails the required return, so reject under the standard rule.
questions.source: Original question 31; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [32] Which set of identities is correct?
questions.explanation:
π=TR-TC; TR=P× Q; TC=VC× Q+FC

Profit = revenue − cost; revenue = price × quantity; total cost = unit variable cost × quantity + fixed cost. Here VC means variable cost per unit.
questions.source: Original question 32; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [33] A firm reports a positive accounting profit, but the return is below what the owner could earn from the next-best alternative. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: The project necessarily maximises shareholder wealth
Economic profit may be negative because opportunity cost is not covered
Opportunity cost is irrelevant once accounting profit is positive

questions.explanation: Implicit opportunity costs can exceed the positive accounting profit.
questions.source: Original question 33; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [34] Which statement correctly distinguishes real and nominal required rates of return?

options.text: It is conceptually determined by inflation alone
A real required return reflects opportunity cost, time preference and risk; a nominal required return also allows for expected inflation
It must always equal the risk-free rate
It falls automatically as investment risk rises

questions.explanation: A real required return reflects opportunity cost, time preference and risk. A nominal required return also allows for expected inflation; cash flows and rates must use consistent nominal or real terms.
questions.source: Original question 34; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [35] Which management decision would most directly increase shareholder value, all else equal?

options.text: Increasing expected costs without changing revenue
Delaying the same cash flow while keeping risk unchanged
Increasing expected future cash returns without increasing the required return
Raising the discount rate applied to unchanged cash flows

questions.explanation: Larger expected returns at the same required return increase present value.
questions.source: Original question 35; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [M1] An investment pays €1,210 at the end of Year 2 and nothing else. At a 10% annual discount rate, what is its present value?
questions.source: Original question M1; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [M2] A project costs €1,000 today and pays €660 at the end of each of Years 1 and 2. There are no other cash flows. At a 10% required return, what are its NPV and the standard investment decision?
questions.explanation: PV of inflows = 660/1.10 + 660/1.10² = €1,145.45. NPV = €145.45, so accept under the standard NPV rule.
questions.source: Original question M2; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [M3] You invest €800 for three years at 5% interest compounded annually, with no withdrawals. What is the future value, rounded to cents?
questions.source: Original question M3; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [36] A firm expects profits per share of €4, €5 and €6 in Years 1–3. Investors require a return of 10%. What is the present value of one share?
questions.source: Original question 36; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [37] A company expects profits per share of €8, €9 and €10 in Years 1–3. The required return is 8%. What is the present value of one share?
questions.explanation: €8/1.08 + €9/1.08² + €10/1.08³ = €23.061779 ≈ €23.06. Canvas marks €25.09, which is incorrect. Sum unrounded values before rounding.
questions.source: Original question 37; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [38] Holding expected future profits constant, what is the effect of an increase in investors’ required rate of return on the current value of a share?

options.text: It first increases and then reduces the share value

questions.explanation: A higher required return lowers the present value of unchanged positive future profits.
questions.source: Original question 38; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [39] A firm sells 2,000 units at €25 per unit. What is total revenue?
questions.source: Original question 39; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [40] A firm’s total revenue is €120,000 and it sells 4,000 units. What is the price per unit?
questions.source: Original question 40; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [41] A firm produces 5,000 units, has a variable cost of €12 per unit and fixed costs of €20,000. What is total cost?
questions.source: Original question 41; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [42] A firm sells 10,000 units at €30 each. Variable cost is €18 per unit and fixed costs are €60,000. What is profit?
questions.source: Original question 42; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [43] A firm sells at €40 per unit, has a variable cost of €25 per unit and fixed costs of €50,000. What is profit at an output of 6,000 units?
questions.explanation: (€40 − €25) × 6,000 − €50,000 = €40,000. Canvas has two identical €40,000 options; the page retains one and uses €50,000 as the other distractor.
questions.source: Original question 43; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [44] A firm’s price is €50, variable cost is €30 per unit and fixed costs are €100,000. What output gives zero profit?
questions.source: Original question 44; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [45] Which statement best captures the shareholder wealth-maximisation model?

options.text: Shareholder wealth is determined only by the firm’s fixed costs
The objective is to maximise sales regardless of costs
Shareholder wealth is related to the present value of expected future cash returns
The objective is to maximise current-period accounting profit only

questions.explanation: Shareholder value is linked to discounted expected future cash returns.
questions.source: Original question 45; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [M4] A firm charges €35 per unit, incurs €21 variable cost per unit and has €42,000 fixed costs. Assuming every unit produced is sold, what output gives zero profit?
questions.explanation: Break-even output = 42,000/(35−21) = 3,000 units.
questions.source: Original question M4; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [81] In any market where units sell at a common price, total revenue is price:

options.text: Divided by the price elasticity of demand
Multiplied by quantity minus production costs

questions.explanation: TR = P × Q. Subtracting costs gives profit.
questions.source: Original question 81; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting

questions.stem: [Q2] An Irish SME pays €100,000 today for a machine generating €60,000 at the end of each of the next two years, with no scrap value. At a 10% discount rate, which conclusion is closest?

options.text: NPV is approximately +€9,091, because only year two is discounted.
NPV is +€20,000, because discounting is irrelevant over two years.
NPV is approximately +€4,132; accept if risk and other assumptions are adequately reflected.

questions.explanation: NPV = −100,000 + 60,000/1.10 + 60,000/1.10² = approximately +€4,132.23. A positive NPV supports acceptance if the required return and assumptions are appropriate.
questions.source: Original question Q2; Lecture #2 — Goals of the firm, shareholder wealth and discounting; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

chapters.title: The Market
chapters.description: Market coordination, price signals, demand, supply and equilibrium.

questions.stem: [46] Hardware shops charge higher prices for snow shovels after a big snowstorm. What role do prices play in the snow-shovel market?

options.text: In an emergency, prices must remain fixed; therefore, prices do not play a role in this case
Higher prices incentivise distributors to ship more snow shovels into the area to meet the increased demand
Prices signal when price gouging is taking place so authorities can step in to prevent it
In such a natural disaster, prices do not efficiently guide the invisible hand

questions.explanation: Higher prices encourage suppliers to direct additional stock towards increased demand.
questions.source: Original question 46; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [47] In the competitive-market model without relevant market failures, which statement best describes the role of price signals?

options.text: Require every participant to know the full cause of each price change
Replace individual choices with a central production plan
Communicate scarcity, coordinate decentralised choices and provide incentives to adjust
Guarantee efficient outcomes even with externalities and market power

questions.explanation: All three statements describe price signals within the competitive-market framework; this depends on the absence of relevant market failures.
questions.source: Original question 47; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [48] Commuters in Beijing find it difficult to get a cab at rush hour while hundreds of cabs lie idle outside cab companies. Demand and fuel prices have risen, but the government has left the base fare unchanged. What government action is likely to correct the situation?

options.text: Lift the price control on the base fare for cabs
Restrict the entry of new cabs

questions.explanation: Removing the binding fare control allows price to adjust to demand and supply conditions.
questions.source: Original question 48; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [49] In a competitive market economy, how do profits and losses guide resource allocation?

options.text: Losses attract entry while profits encourage firms to leave
Profits attract resources towards more-valued uses; losses encourage resources to move elsewhere
Profits prevent new firms entering a market
Falling consumer valuations necessarily increase producers’ returns

questions.explanation: Profits attract resources and entry; losses encourage reallocation or exit.
questions.source: Original question 49; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [50] Which of the following is true of the market economy?

options.text: It generates lower economic output than a command economy
It aligns incentives but fails to coordinate economic agents
It inherently facilitates coordination between economic agents and aligns incentives
It facilitates coordination between economic agents but misaligns incentives

questions.explanation: Prices help coordinate decentralised decisions and align incentives in the market model.
questions.source: Original question 50; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [51] The concept of the invisible hand was introduced by:
questions.explanation: Adam Smith introduced the invisible-hand concept.
questions.source: Original question 51; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [52] Within the introductory competitive-market model, how can self-interested competition benefit consumers?

options.text: Competition rewards higher costs without any quality gain
Competitive pressure can encourage efficiency and better offerings while constraining prices
The invisible hand requires government to assign output quotas to every firm
Competition guarantees that no firm ever makes a loss

questions.explanation: Competitive pressure can reward efficiency and useful product improvements and constrain prices. These are model mechanisms, not guarantees in every real market.
questions.source: Original question 52; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [53] The concept of the invisible hand refers to:

options.text: A central planner assigning production quotas
Individuals making decisions in their own self-interest
The Federal Reserve setting interest rates
A rule requiring identical profits in every firm

questions.explanation: Decentralised self-interested decisions can coordinate through prices.
questions.source: Original question 53; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [54] The concept of self-interest, as understood in the invisible-hand model, refers to:
questions.explanation: Self-regarding means pursuing one’s own objectives or welfare; it does not require selfishness.
questions.source: Original question 54; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [60] There are five students who are looking to buy one second-hand textbook each. Their willingness to pay is £5, £6, £8, £12 and £15, respectively. Which statement is correct?

options.text: To sell three books, the maximum price that can be charged is £8.
The student with a willingness to pay of £15 is the richest.
If a seller is one of many identical sellers and his reservation price is £8, then he is guaranteed to sell his textbook.
Their willingness to pay indicates an upward-sloping demand curve.

questions.explanation: At £8, three students are willing to buy; above £8, only two are. Willingness to pay does not reveal wealth or guarantee a sale.
questions.source: Original question 60; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [62] The textbook market has demand P = 20 − 0.5Q and supply P = 2 + 0.25Q, with price in dollars. These equations replace the diagram missing from Canvas. Which statement is correct?

options.text: At a price of $6, there is excess demand of 4 books.
There are sellers willing to give away their textbooks for free.
At a price of $12, all books offered for sale will be sold.

questions.explanation: 20 − 0.5Q = 2 + 0.25Q gives Q = 24 and P = $8. At $6, Qd = 28 and Qs = 16, so excess demand is 12 books. The replacement uses the matching CORE textbook-market model. Source model (https://books.core-econ.org/the-economy-v1/book/text/08.html#82-the-market-and-the-equilibrium-price)
questions.source: Original question 62; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [63] The source tables compare average wheat prices in 1838–45 with maximum prices in 1845–48, relative to silver. A poor harvest occurred in 1845. Compare countries with violent revolution in 1848 with those without revolution: Austria 52.9 → 104.0 and Hungary 39.0 → 92.3; England 115.3 → 134.7 and Sweden 75.8 → 81.4. Which statement is supported?

options.text: A downward shift of the supply curve caused the price hike.
A high average price of wheat caused violent revolution.
Countries with a violent revolution necessarily had a more inelastic demand curve.
There is a positive correlation between large wheat-price hikes and the incidence of violent revolution.

questions.explanation: The price changes are about 96.6%, 136.7%, 16.8% and 7.4%, respectively. The data support an association, not proof of causation or demand elasticity. Canvas omitted the tables; representative source rows are supplied here. Complete source table (https://books.core-econ.org/the-economy-v1/book/text/08.html#exercise-8-5-the-price-of-bread)
questions.source: Original question 63; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [64] Which of the following is not one of the major factors that shifts the supply curve when it changes?

options.text: Prices of inputs used in production

questions.explanation: Consumer income shifts demand. Input costs, seller numbers and relevant expectations can shift supply.
questions.source: Original question 64; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [65] The wine industry relies on unskilled labour to pick grapes. Other things equal, an increase in immigration that increases the available labour supply and reduces labour costs will shift the supply curve of wine:

options.text: The wine market’s demand curve shifts left instead

questions.explanation: Lower labour costs make more wine profitable to supply at each price. The cost assumption makes the original question explicit.
questions.source: Original question 65; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [66] Which of the following is not one of the major factors that shifts the demand curve when it changes?

options.text: The price of the good itself

questions.explanation: A change in the good’s own price causes a movement along its demand curve.
questions.source: Original question 66; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [67] National income increases by 20%, causing a 20% increase in houses demanded at every price. Assume demand slopes downward and the unchanged supply curve slopes upward with finite elasticity. The equilibrium number of houses traded is likely to:
questions.explanation: The demand shift raises price; this reduces part of the quantity increase. Perfectly elastic supply would instead allow a 20% increase; perfectly inelastic supply would leave quantity unchanged. The original omitted the supply assumption.
questions.source: Original question 67; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [68] Which factor is expected to cause the demand curve for coffee to shift to the right?

options.text: A higher tax on the sale of tea, a substitute for coffee
A fall in the manufacturing cost of coffee
A higher personal tax on the income of all consumers
An increase in the supply of coffee due to better weather

questions.explanation: A tax that raises the price of tea encourages substitution towards coffee. Coffee production costs and weather affect coffee supply.
questions.source: Original question 68; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [69] Z is a normal good. Its equilibrium price and quantity were €25 and 60 units in 2020. In 2021 they increased to €35 and 70 units. Other things equal, which change could explain this?

options.text: A shift of demand for Z to the right
A shift of demand for Z to the left
A shift of supply of Z to the right
A shift of supply of Z to the left

questions.explanation: A rightward demand shift raises both equilibrium price and quantity with unchanged upward-sloping supply.
questions.source: Original question 69; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [70] Z is a normal good. Its equilibrium price and quantity were €25 and 60 units in 2020. In 2021 they decreased to €15 and 50 units. Other things equal, which change could explain this?

options.text: A shift of demand for Z to the left
A shift of supply of Z to the left
A shift of supply of Z to the right
A shift of demand for Z to the right

questions.explanation: A leftward demand shift lowers both price and quantity with unchanged supply.
questions.source: Original question 70; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [71] From 2001 to 2011, quinoa output and prices rose following stronger overseas demand. In the demand-and-supply model, with other influences unchanged, which combined interpretation is correct?

options.text: The rise proves that every resident of the producing countries is better off
Stronger demand can explain higher price and output, and higher prices encourage production elsewhere
A supply contraction alone explains both higher price and higher output
Higher prices prevent other countries from expanding output

questions.explanation: A rightward demand shift raises equilibrium price and output. Higher prices encourage additional production elsewhere, but consumers who buy quinoa can be worse off.
questions.source: Original question 71; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [72] New technology shifts the bread supply curve right/down, while demand and the number of bakeries remain unchanged. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bakeries’ marginal cost of production has fallen.
Excess demand at the original price has led to the fall in equilibrium price.
The more elastic the demand curve, the larger the fall in price.
There has been an increase in demand.

questions.explanation: The technology reduces costs. At the old price there is excess supply. The stated shift makes the diagram-based question self-contained.
questions.source: Original question 72; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [73] In the standard competitive model without externalities, demand shifts right/up because consumers are richer and supply shifts right/down because marginal costs fall. Which combined outcome follows?

options.text: Price must fall; quantity and total surplus are ambiguous
Quantity and total surplus rise; the price change is ambiguous
Price and quantity must both fall
Total surplus falls whenever supply and demand both rise

questions.explanation: Both shifts increase equilibrium quantity. Higher willingness to pay and lower production costs increase gains from trade, while their price effects oppose each other.
questions.source: Original question 73; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [M6] Demand is Qd=150−5P and supply is Qs=30+3P, where P is euros per unit. Which equilibrium pair is correct?
questions.explanation: 150−5P = 30+3P gives P = €15 and Q = 75.
questions.source: Original question M6; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [M7] A market has demand Qd=150−5P and supply Qs=30+3P. If price is held at €10, what is the market imbalance?
questions.explanation: At €10, Qd = 100 and Qs = 60, so excess demand is 40 units.
questions.source: Original question M7; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [M8] Supply is Qs=30+3P. Demand changes from Qd=150−5P to Qd=190−5P. What are the new equilibrium price and quantity?
questions.explanation: 190−5P = 30+3P gives P = €20 and Q = 90.
questions.source: Original question M8; Lecture #3 — Market

questions.stem: [Q3] A sudden shortage of cocoa raises its price. A confectionery firm switches to recipes using less cocoa without learning why the shortage arose. Which interpretation most closely reflects Hayek’s argument?

options.text: Only a central authority can coordinate a response to the shortage.
Price signals remove scarcity rather than changing responses to it.
Prices communicate dispersed information and induce economising without every decision-maker knowing the underlying cause.
A higher cocoa price proves that demand must have increased.

questions.explanation: Hayek’s price mechanism communicates scarcity and coordinates economising without each person knowing the underlying disruption.
questions.source: Original question Q3; Lecture #3 — Market; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [Q4] A profitable market attracts new independent suppliers over time. Assuming demand and input costs do not change, which sequence is most consistent with competition and Smith’s market coordination?

options.text: Market supply shifts left, price rises, and profits necessarily increase indefinitely.
Individual firms gain permanent pricing power simply because more firms enter.
Market supply shifts right, equilibrium price falls, and above-normal economic profits tend to be competed away.
Demand shifts right, price rises, and entry is discouraged.

questions.explanation: Entry expands market supply. With demand and input costs unchanged, price falls and above-normal economic profits tend to be competed away.
questions.source: Original question Q4; Lecture #3 — Market; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [Q5] Aldi estimates demand Qd = 150 − 3P and supply Qs = 30 + 2P for a wine. A €5 per-bottle tax on suppliers changes supply to Qs = 30 + 2(P − 5). What are the new consumer price and equilibrium quantity?
questions.explanation: Tax-adjusted supply is Qs = 20+2P. Equating this with 150−3P gives P = €26 and Q = 72.
questions.source: Original question Q5; Lecture #3 — Market; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [Q6] In the figure, both demand and supply shift vertically upwards by €12 at every quantity (D0→D1 and S0→S1). What happens to equilibrium?

options.text: Equilibrium price rises while equilibrium quantity remains unchanged.
Equilibrium quantity rises while price is unchanged.
Both price and quantity are unchanged.

questions.explanation: Equal vertical shifts add €12 to the price at the original intersection quantity. Quantity is unchanged; equilibrium price rises.
questions.source: Original question Q6; Lecture #3 — Market; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

image.alt: Demand D0 and supply S0, and their upward-shifted curves D1 and S1, on price and quantity axes.

questions.stem: [Q7] A fall in the price of a substitute raises demand for the substitute and reduces demand for takeaway pizza. At the same time, higher energy costs reduce pizza supply. Which outcome can be predicted with certainty?

options.text: Equilibrium price rises and quantity rises.
Equilibrium quantity of pizza falls; the direction of the price change is ambiguous.
Both equilibrium price and quantity necessarily fall.
Equilibrium price falls and quantity rises.

questions.explanation: Both lower demand and lower supply reduce equilibrium quantity. Their effects on price oppose one another, making price ambiguous.
questions.source: Original question Q7; Lecture #3 — Market; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [Q8] A market has Qd = 120 − 2P and Qs = 3P − 30. The government imposes a binding maximum price of €24. What shortage results?
questions.explanation: At €24, Qd = 72 and Qs = 42, so the shortage is 30 units.
questions.source: Original question Q8; Lecture #3 — Market; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [P2] A competitive market has inverse demand P=30−0.2Q and original inverse supply S₀: P=0.1Q. Supply changes to S₁: P=6+0.1Q, with demand unchanged. Using Graph 2 and the equations, what are the new equilibrium price and quantity?
questions.explanation: Equating new supply and demand gives 30−0.2Q=6+0.1Q, so Q=80 and P=€14.

questions.stem: [OS1] Consider a competitive market for paint with downward-sloping demand and upward-sloping supply. Cost-saving inventions make paint cheaper to produce, while longer-lasting paint means buildings need repainting less often. Both changes occur together; all other factors are unchanged. What can be predicted about the new equilibrium price and quantity of paint?

options.text: Price falls; the change in quantity is ambiguous.
Price is ambiguous; quantity necessarily falls.
Both price and quantity necessarily rise.

questions.explanation: Lower production costs shift supply right; less frequent repainting shifts demand left. Both lower price, while their quantity effects oppose one another.

Hailstorms increase the need to repaint buildings and simultaneously force several paint factories to close. All other factors are unchanged. Which result for the new equilibrium is certain?

options.text: Price rises, while quantity may rise or fall.
Quantity rises, while price may rise or fall.

questions.explanation: Greater repainting demand shifts demand right, while factory closures shift supply left. Both raise price; quantity depends on the relative shifts.

questions.stem: [OS3] Cars become more fuel-efficient, so drivers need less oil-derived fuel to travel the same distance. Assume total driving is unchanged, oil supply slopes upward, oil demand slopes downward and no other conditions change. What happens in the oil market?

options.text: Demand shifts left; equilibrium price and quantity fall.
The oil demand curve does not shift; only a movement along it occurs.

questions.explanation: With driving unchanged, greater fuel efficiency reduces oil demand. A leftward demand shift lowers equilibrium price and quantity with unchanged upward-sloping supply.

questions.stem: [OS4] Jet fuel is an input used to provide airline flights, and its price rises. Assume demand for flights slopes downward and remains unchanged, supply slopes upward, and all other conditions are unchanged. What is the expected effect on flight supply, fares and the quantity of flights?

options.text: Flight supply shifts right; fares fall.
Flight demand shifts left; fares fall.
Flight demand shifts right; fares rise.
Flight supply shifts left; fares rise and the quantity of flights falls.

questions.explanation: Higher jet-fuel input costs shift flight supply left. Unchanged downward-sloping demand then yields higher fares and fewer flights.

chapters.title: Consumers & Incentives
chapters.description: Marginal utility, consumer surplus and demand elasticities.

questions.stem: [74] A restaurant increases its pizza price from €12 to €15. Sales fall from 200 to 160 pizzas per week. Using initial values as the percentage-change base, what is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: Quantity change: (160 − 200)/200 = −20%. Price change: (15 − 12)/12 = 25%. PED = −20/25 = −0.8. Using the midpoint method instead gives −1.0; the method must be specified.
questions.source: Original question 74; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [75] A drought reduces the available quantity of wheat by 20%. If PED is −0.5, use the percentage-change elasticity approximation to estimate the price increase needed for quantity demanded to fall by 20%.
questions.explanation: %ΔQ = PED × %ΔP, so %ΔP = −20%/−0.5 = 40%. This is the introductory approximation, not an exact large-change prediction from a constant-elasticity demand function.
questions.source: Original question 75; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [76] At an interior optimum with diminishing marginal benefits, a consumer’s satisfaction is maximised when marginal benefit per euro is equal across goods because:

options.text: Any small reallocation of expenditure towards either good would fail to improve satisfaction.
Any shift in consumption towards either good violates the budget constraint.
Her preferences become invalid when marginal benefits per euro differ.
Unequal ratios imply that she has insufficient income to maximise satisfaction.

questions.explanation: If one good yielded more benefit per euro, shifting spending towards it would improve satisfaction. The interior-optimum assumption avoids corner-solution exceptions.
questions.source: Original question 76; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [77] Michael has an exam tomorrow. Total expected extra marks from studying for 1–5 hours are 10, 14, 18, 21 and 23; total marks lost through tiredness are 0, 3, 7, 12 and 18. Which option lists all study durations that maximise net expected marks?
questions.explanation: Net expected marks at 1–5 hours are 10, 11, 11, 9 and 5. Both 2 and 3 hours maximise net benefit; the third hour adds equal marginal benefit and cost.
questions.source: Original question 77; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [78] Mary is willing to pay at most €40 for a bracelet. She buys it for €22.50. What consumer surplus does she gain?
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus = willingness to pay − price = €40 − €22.50 = €17.50.
questions.source: Original question 78; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [79] The price of bags rises from €11 to €13 and quantity demanded falls from 56 to 52. A further table row gives €15 and 44 bags. Using the initial point (€11, 56) and the €11 → €13 interval, what is the absolute price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: ΔQ = −4 and ΔP = 2. Initial-point estimate: (−4/2) × (11/56) = −0.392857, absolute value ≈ 0.39. None of the original options was correct. The midpoint/arc value is about 0.44, which was incorrectly mixed into the original point-elasticity question.
questions.source: Original question 79; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [80] Last year John bought 50 pounds of mincemeat when household income was €40,000. This year income was €30,000 and he bought 60 pounds. All else constant, his income elasticity is:

options.text: Negative, so mincemeat is an inferior good for John.
Positive, so mincemeat is a normal good for John.
Negative, so mincemeat is a normal good for John.
Positive, so mincemeat is an inferior good for John.

questions.explanation: Quantity rises as income falls. Using initial values gives (10/50)/(−10,000/40,000) = −0.8.
questions.source: Original question 80; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [82] The cross-price elasticity of food demand with respect to the price of entertainment is −0.7. If entertainment prices rise by 20%, the percentage-change approximation predicts that food quantity demanded:

options.text: Rises by 0.14%, and the goods are substitutes.
Falls by 14%, and the goods are complements.
Falls by 14%, and the goods are substitutes.
Falls by 0.14%, and the goods are complements.

questions.explanation: %ΔQfood = −0.7 × 20% = −14%. A negative cross-price elasticity identifies complements.
questions.source: Original question 82; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [83] Holding other forces constant, a rise in motor-fuel prices produces a larger fall in quantity demanded over ten years than immediately because:

options.text: Buyers are more sensitive to price changes when given more time to respond.
Fuel demand becomes perfectly inelastic as time passes.
Buyers are less sensitive to price changes when given more time to react.
Buyers necessarily have substantially more income after ten years.

questions.explanation: People have more time to change vehicles, travel habits or location, making long-run demand more elastic.
questions.source: Original question 83; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [84] You and your housemate each eat three packets of Pot Noodles weekly. After your incomes rise, you buy more while your housemate buys fewer and substitutes preferred foods. Your income elasticity and your housemate’s are, respectively:
questions.explanation: The same product can be normal for one person and inferior for another.
questions.source: Original question 84; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [M9] Price rises from €20 to €24 and quantity demanded falls from 150 to 105 units. What is signed PED and its classification? Use initial values as the percentage-change base.
questions.explanation: Quantity falls 30% and price rises 20%, using initial values. PED = −30/20 = −1.5; demand is elastic.
questions.source: Original question M9; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [M10] The price of Y rises from €10 to €12 while quantity demanded of X falls from 80 to 72 units, other things equal. What is X's cross-price elasticity with respect to Y's price, and what relationship does it indicate? Use initial values as the percentage-change base.
questions.explanation: Quantity of X falls 10% while Y’s price rises 20%. Cross-price elasticity = −0.5, indicating complements.
questions.source: Original question M10; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [M11] Income rises from €2,000 to €2,200 and quantity demanded rises from 50 to 54 units, other things equal. What is income elasticity and the good's classification over this change? Use initial values as the percentage-change base.
questions.explanation: Quantity rises 8% while income rises 10%. Income elasticity = +0.8, so the good is normal over this change.
questions.source: Original question M11; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [Q9] A supplier cuts price from €20 to €18; sales rise from 100 to 130 units. Using the original price and quantity as the base for percentage changes, which combination is closest?
questions.explanation: Quantity rises 30% and price falls 10%, giving PED = −3. Revenue rises from €2,000 to €2,340.
questions.source: Original question Q9; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [Q10] A restaurant raises menu prices by 8%. Quantity demanded falls by 4%, while average variable cost per meal is unchanged. Which statement is defensible?

options.text: Demand is elastic and revenue must fall.
Revenue must fall because demand slopes downward.
Revenue increases approximately, but the effect on profit cannot be established without cost and quantity information.

questions.explanation: Revenue is multiplied by 1.08×0.96 = 1.0368, a 3.68% increase. The stated information does not fully specify the change in all costs, so it does not establish a particular profit change.
questions.source: Original question Q10; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [Q11] The price of Brand A coffee increases by 12%; sales of Brand B coffee rise by 9%; sales of biscuits fall by 6%. Using the simple percentage-change method, which is correct?

options.text: Cross-price elasticity of B with respect to A is −0.75, suggesting complements.
Cross-price elasticity of B with respect to A is +0.75, suggesting substitutes.
Own-price elasticity of A is +1.33, implying a Giffen good.
Income elasticity of biscuits is −0.50, suggesting an inferior good.

questions.explanation: Cross-price elasticity of B with respect to A is 9%/12% = +0.75, consistent with substitutes.
questions.source: Original question Q11; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [Q12] The figure shows a competitive market. At the equilibrium, what is consumer surplus?
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the triangle above the €40 price and below demand: ½×20×(80−40) = €400.
questions.source: Original question Q12; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [Q13] A student values successive café lunches at €16, €13, €10 and €7, and each lunch costs €9. Assuming independent marginal values and no other constraints, how many lunches maximise consumer surplus?
questions.explanation: The first three lunches have marginal values above €9; the fourth is worth only €7. Three lunches maximise consumer surplus.
questions.source: Original question Q13; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [P3] The price of product Y rises from €8 to €8.80. Other influences are held constant, and quantity demanded of product X rises from 200 to 230 units. Using initial-value percentage changes, which option gives the cross-price elasticity of demand for X with respect to Y's price and the relationship it indicates?
questions.explanation: X quantity rises 15% and Y price rises 10%. Cross-price elasticity is +1.5, indicating substitutes.
questions.source: Original question P3; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7

questions.stem: [OS7] A pharmaceutical firm wants to increase revenue from its hair-growth treatment. Demand has an absolute price elasticity of 1.4 at the current price. For a small price change with other conditions unchanged, which recommendation follows?

options.text: Raise price because demand is inelastic.
Lower price because demand is elastic.
Keep price unchanged because demand is unit elastic.
Lower quantity independently of price because revenue is fixed.

questions.explanation: At absolute PED 1.4, demand is elastic. A small price reduction raises quantity proportionately more and increases revenue, other things equal.
questions.source: Original question OS7; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7; OpenStax adaptation: https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/5-self-check-questions

questions.stem: [OS8] Average annual income for a group of consumers rises from $25,000 to $38,000, while annual bread purchases per consumer fall from 30 to 22 loaves. Assume prices and other influences on bread demand are unchanged. Using the initial income and quantity as the percentage-change denominators, which income-elasticity result and classification are correct?

options.text: Income elasticity is about +1.95; bread is normal.
Income elasticity is about −1.95; bread is inferior.
Income elasticity is about +0.51; bread is inferior.
Income elasticity is about −0.51; bread is inferior.

questions.explanation: Initial-value income elasticity = ((22−30)/30)/((38,000−25,000)/25,000) ≈ −0.5128. The negative sign identifies an inferior good.
questions.source: Original question OS8; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7; OpenStax adaptation: https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/5-self-check-questions

questions.stem: [OS9] The cross-price elasticity of apple demand with respect to the orange price is +0.4. If orange prices fall by 3%, what is the approximate change in apple demand, other things equal?
questions.explanation: The percentage-change approximation gives 0.4×(−3%) = −1.2% for apple demand.
questions.source: Original question OS9; Consumers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #6–7; OpenStax adaptation: https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/5-self-check-questions

questions.stem: [OS10] José has a total budget of $56 to spend on T-shirts and cinema tickets. Each T-shirt costs $14 and each ticket for one movie costs $7. He cannot borrow or spend more than his budget; spending exactly $56 is allowed. A bundle means one proposed combination of T-shirts and tickets. Which bundle is unaffordable?
questions.explanation: Bundle C costs 2×$14 + 5×$7 = $63, above $56. The other proposed bundles cost $56 each.

questions.stem: [M5] A business earns €160,000 revenue and pays €100,000 explicit costs. Its owner's forgone salary is €70,000, the only implicit cost. What are accounting profit and economic profit, respectively?
questions.explanation: Accounting profit = 160,000−100,000 = €60,000; economic profit also deducts €70,000 forgone salary, giving −€10,000.
questions.source: Original question M5; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [55] A professional leaves a €120,000 salary to start a business. Which cost is most relevant to the economist but may not appear in the firm's accounts?
questions.explanation: The forgone salary is an implicit opportunity cost.
questions.source: Original question 55; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [56] For an audit office, why might a partner's salary be treated differently as a fixed or variable cost?

options.text: Because the classification can depend on the time horizon and how the partner's workload changes with output
Because all salaries are always fixed
Because partner salaries are never costs
Because fixed costs always change with output

questions.explanation: Cost classification depends on the relevant time horizon and whether the expense varies with output.
questions.source: Original question 56; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [57] A firm's total cost rises from €10,000 to €10,600 when output rises from 100 to 120 units. What is the marginal cost per additional unit?
questions.source: Original question 57; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [58] At the current output, a firm's marginal revenue is €900 and marginal cost is €700. What should the firm do if it wants to increase profit?

options.text: Keep output unchanged because MR is irrelevant

questions.explanation: MR − MC = €900 − €700 = €200 for an additional unit, so expanding output can raise profit.
questions.source: Original question 58; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [85] More students arrive, shifting textbook demand right/up while an upward-sloping supply curve remains unchanged. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Every buyer who would have bought before the shift will still buy after it.
The more inelastic supply is, the larger the increase in quantity traded.
There has been an increase in supply.
The more elastic supply is, the smaller the price rise.

questions.explanation: Supply elasticity governs how much adjustment occurs through quantity rather than price.
questions.source: Original question 85; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [86] For straight-line bread demand and supply curves, keep their intersection (equilibrium price and output) unchanged while varying slopes. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A less elastic demand curve leads to smaller consumer surplus.
A less elastic supply curve leads to larger producer surplus.
A more elastic demand curve leads to smaller producer surplus when supply is unchanged.
Consumer and producer surplus do not depend on curve elasticities.

questions.explanation: Steeper supply increases the area between price and supply to the left of equilibrium. The linear-curve assumption makes the original diagram-based comparison precise.
questions.source: Original question 86; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [91] As positive output rises, average fixed cost:
questions.explanation: AFC = FC/Q; an unchanged fixed cost is spread over more units.
questions.source: Original question 91; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [92] When land prices increase from €6,000 to €10,000 per acre but acreage supplied is unchanged, the price elasticity of supply over this change is:

options.text: Determined by a low opportunity cost

questions.explanation: %ΔQs = 0, so PES = 0: perfectly inelastic supply over the observed range. The original stem asked for a property of supply but offered bare numbers.
questions.source: Original question 92; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [93] Is it possible for accounting profit to be positive and economic profit to be negative?

options.text: No, accounting and economic profit are identical.
Yes, when total explicit and implicit opportunity costs exceed revenue even though explicit costs alone do not.
No, economic profit must always exceed accounting profit.
Yes, simply because fixed costs are a small proportion of total costs.

questions.explanation: Accounting profit subtracts explicit costs. Economic profit also subtracts implicit opportunity costs.
questions.source: Original question 93; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [94] For a perfectly competitive firm that operates in the short run, an interior profit-maximising output on the rising part of MC satisfies:

options.text: Price = marginal cost = average total cost

questions.explanation: P = MR = MC is the output rule, provided operating covers variable costs. Equality with ATC is not required in the short run. The original four options omitted the general correct rule.
questions.source: Original question 94; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [95] According to marginal analysis, optimal decision-making involves:

options.text: Taking actions until total benefit equals total cost
Taking actions whenever marginal benefit is positive
Taking actions only if marginal cost is zero
Taking actions while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost; being indifferent to an increment when they are equal

questions.explanation: Compare additional benefit with additional cost. Equality adds zero net benefit and can produce tied optima.
questions.source: Original question 95; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [96] If marginal cost is below average total cost, an increase in output causes average total cost to:
questions.explanation: Adding units that cost less than the current average lowers that average.
questions.source: Original question 96; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [M12] At Q=200, fixed cost is €600 and total variable cost is €1,400. Which set gives AFC, AVC and ATC, respectively?
questions.source: Original question M12; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [M13] With capital fixed, hiring one more worker increases output from 240 to 280 units and total cost from €1,800 to €1,920. What are that worker's marginal product and the marginal cost per extra output unit over this interval?
questions.explanation: Marginal product is 280−240 = 40 units. Marginal cost per additional unit is (1,920−1,800)/40 = €3.
questions.source: Original question M13; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [M14] A price-taking firm can produce Q=0, 1, 2 or 3 units. Total costs are €50, €62, €80 and €106, respectively. Price is €20 per unit and the €50 fixed cost is unavoidable. Which listed output maximises short-run profit?
questions.explanation: Profits at Q = 0,1,2,3 are −€50, −€42, −€40 and −€46. Two units minimise the loss and maximise profit among these choices.
questions.source: Original question M14; Sellers and Incentives lecture slides; Lectures #7–8

questions.stem: [103] An accounting firm charges €1,200 per client, has average economic cost of €900 per client and serves 100 clients. What is economic profit?

questions.explanation: The rising MC curve meets P = MR = €14 at Q = 20. Under the operating assumption, this is the profit-maximising output.

Marginal cost over the extra ten loaves is €6 per loaf, below initial ATC, so ATC falls over that range.
Marginal cost is €60 per loaf, above ATC.

What are its annual accounting profit and economic profit, respectively?
