chapters.title: Market Structure
chapters.description: Perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and Porter’s Five Forces.

questions.stem: [59] In perfect competition, why is marginal revenue equal to price for an individual firm?

options.text: The firm is a price taker and can sell additional output at the market price
The firm chooses the market price

questions.explanation: A price-taking firm receives the same market price for an extra unit, so MR = P.
questions.source: Original question 59; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [61] Which of the following markets can generally be considered competitive in the price-taking model?

options.text: Etsy, a platform where unique handcrafted products are offered for sale.
The market for tickets to a particular rock concert.

questions.explanation: Milk is the best approximation here to a standardised product with many suppliers; the alternatives involve differentiation, unique events or patent protection. This is a model approximation, not a claim that every milk market is perfectly competitive.
questions.source: Original question 61; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [97] Assume a bakery is a price taker in a perfectly competitive bread market. Market demand slopes down; the bakery has fixed costs and rising marginal cost. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bakery can ensure that its price exceeds average cost.
The bakery faces a flat demand curve at the market price.
The bakery’s supply curve is horizontal.
The bakery always earns positive economic rent.

questions.explanation: The firm can sell at the given market price, so its own demand is horizontal. Merely having many bakeries would not establish price-taking without the added assumption.
questions.source: Original question 97; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [98] A monopolist faces P = 100 − Q and MR = 100 − 2Q. Marginal cost is constant at €20. What output maximises profit? Assume the firm operates, output is continuous and there are no capacity constraints.
questions.source: Original question 98; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [99] For the monopolist with P = 100 − Q, MR = 100 − 2Q and MC = €20, what price is charged at the profit-maximising output? Assume the firm operates, output is continuous and there are no capacity constraints.
questions.explanation: Q = 40; substitute into demand: P = 100 − 40 = €60.
questions.source: Original question 99; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [100] For a monopolist, Q = 40, price = €60 and average economic cost = €35. What is economic profit?
questions.source: Original question 100; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [101] A pharmaceutical company holds a patent for a drug. What does the patent primarily represent in market-structure terms?

options.text: A legal barrier to entry that can create market power

questions.explanation: Patent protection restricts entry for the protected invention.
questions.source: Original question 101; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [102] A water network has high fixed costs and low marginal costs, making one supplier cheaper than duplicated networks. Which concept describes this?
questions.explanation: One firm can serve the relevant market at lower total cost.
questions.source: Original question 102; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [104] A restaurant in monopolistic competition charges €40 per meal, has average economic cost of €50 and sells 500 meals. What is economic profit?
questions.source: Original question 104; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [105] A monopolistically competitive firm earns positive economic profit and entry is easy. What is the likely long-run effect on its demand?

options.text: Demand shifts left as new firms enter.
Demand shifts right as competitors leave.

questions.explanation: Entrants compete for customers, reducing demand faced by each incumbent.
questions.source: Original question 105; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [106] A restaurant’s reputation and distinctive dining experience allow it to charge €5 more than a similar competitor. What explains this pricing power?
questions.explanation: Customers perceive a difference and may prefer this restaurant.
questions.source: Original question 106; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [107] In long-run monopolistic-competition equilibrium, a firm sells 2,000 units for €25 each and earns zero economic profit. What is average economic cost?
questions.explanation: Zero economic profit requires P = AC, so AC = €25.
questions.source: Original question 107; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [108] Four firms have shares of 35%, 25%, 20% and 20%. What is the two-firm concentration ratio?
questions.explanation: Add the two largest shares: 35% + 25% = 60%.
questions.source: Original question 108; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [109] Five firms have shares of 30%, 25%, 20%, 15% and 10%. What is the three-firm concentration ratio?
questions.source: Original question 109; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [110] An oligopolist considers cutting its price. Which question matters most because of oligopolistic competition?

options.text: How are competitors likely to respond?
Will the firm become a price taker?

questions.explanation: A few large firms are strategically interdependent.
questions.source: Original question 110; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [111] Two firms each have 45% of an industry; the remaining firms together have 10%. What is the two-firm concentration ratio?
questions.source: Original question 111; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [112] An oligopolistic industry is profitable and has significant entry barriers. Which factor helps maintain profitability?

options.text: High entry barriers limiting competitive pressure

questions.explanation: Barriers restrict entry that might otherwise compete away economic profit.
questions.source: Original question 112; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [113] A perfectly competitive firm faces P = €50. MC is €30 at Q = 40, €50 at Q = 50 and €70 at Q = 60. Assuming rising MC and that P covers AVC at Q = 50, what output should it choose?
questions.explanation: Choose Q = 50 where P = MC. The AVC assumption rules out shutdown.
questions.source: Original question 113; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [114] A competitive firm produces 500 units at €40 each. MC is €25 and the next units also have MC below €40. What should it do?

options.text: Reduce output because price exceeds average cost.
Increase output because extra units cost less than the price received.
Keep output unchanged because MC is positive.
Stop producing because it is not a monopoly.

questions.explanation: Additional units add positive marginal profit while P = MR exceeds MC.
questions.source: Original question 114; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [115] A perfectly competitive firm sells 1,000 units for €20 each. Average economic cost is €20. What is economic profit?
questions.source: Original question 115; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [116] A commodity producer in perfect competition raises its price from €100 to €105 while identical products remain available for €100. What is the likely outcome?

options.text: It sells more because its price is higher.
It may sell none of its output.

questions.explanation: Buyers can purchase the identical product from rivals for less.
questions.source: Original question 116; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [M15] A single-price monopolist faces P=120−2Q. Which pair correctly gives its total-revenue and marginal-revenue functions? Assume the firm operates, output is continuous and there are no capacity constraints.
questions.explanation: TR = P×Q = 120Q−2Q². Its derivative is MR = 120−4Q.
questions.source: Original question M15; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [M16] A monopolist has P=120−2Q, MR=120−4Q and constant MC=€40. What output and selling price maximise profit? Assume the firm operates, output is continuous and there are no capacity constraints.
questions.explanation: MR = MC gives 120−4Q = 40, hence Q = 20. Demand then gives P = 120−2(20) = €80.
questions.source: Original question M16; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [117] A regional supermarket chain faces customers who can compare prices instantly and switch to competing supermarkets within minutes. Which force is most directly strengthened?
questions.explanation: Easy price comparisons and low switching costs strengthen buyers’ leverage.
questions.source: Original question 117; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [118] A small craft brewery depends on one specialist supplier for a patented canning component. The supplier raises its price and the brewery has no practical alternative. Which force is strongest?
questions.explanation: Dependence on a unique input with no practical alternative gives the supplier leverage.
questions.source: Original question 118; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [119] A city has dozens of similarly sized coffee shops competing through discounts and promotions, while demand is growing slowly. What does this mainly indicate?
questions.explanation: Many similar-sized competitors and slow growth intensify the fight for market share.
questions.source: Original question 119; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [120] An airline serving a domestic route loses passengers when improved intercity rail services become faster and cheaper. Which force best explains the pressure?

options.text: Threat of substitute products or services

questions.explanation: Rail meets the same transport need by a different means, so it is a substitute rather than another airline.
questions.source: Original question 120; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [121] A pharmaceutical company holds a valid patent on a new medicine. How does the patent most directly affect its industry?

options.text: It removes competition from existing firms
It raises barriers to entry, reducing the threat of new entrants

questions.explanation: A patent restricts entry for the protected invention; competing treatments may still exist.
questions.source: Original question 121; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [122] A hotel chain negotiates a large annual laundry contract. Several laundry providers compete for the business, and changing provider is relatively easy. Which outcome is most likely?

options.text: Entry barriers for new hotels necessarily rise
Laundry providers gain greater bargaining power
Threat of substitutes for hotel stays disappears
The hotel chain gains bargaining power as a buyer

questions.explanation: The large contract and easy switching strengthen the hotel’s negotiating position.
questions.source: Original question 122; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [123] A new meal-delivery company can launch using inexpensive software, contract couriers and existing restaurants. What is the most direct implication for established delivery platforms?

options.text: The threat of new entrants may be high

questions.explanation: Low start-up requirements reduce entry barriers and can make entry more likely.
questions.source: Original question 123; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [124] A cinema operator finds that households increasingly prefer streaming films at home rather than buying cinema tickets. Which response best identifies the competitive force?

options.text: Higher supplier power because studios produce films
Higher entry barriers for new cinemas
Greater threat from substitutes because streaming meets a similar entertainment need

questions.explanation: Streaming meets the underlying entertainment need differently, creating substitution pressure.
questions.source: Original question 124; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [125] A furniture manufacturer sells to three national retail chains that together account for 80% of its sales. Each chain can switch to several rival manufacturers. Which force is most concerning?
questions.explanation: Concentrated customers with alternative manufacturers can exert strong buyer power.
questions.source: Original question 125; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [126] An industry has high fixed costs, little product differentiation and declining sales. Under Porter’s framework, which prediction is most plausible?

options.text: Supplier power necessarily falls to zero
Competition between established firms is likely to intensify

questions.explanation: Firms have incentives to fill capacity and compete for a shrinking pool of similar sales.
questions.source: Original question 126; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [Q16] A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − 2Q and marginal cost MC = 20 + 0.5Q. Which output–price pair maximises profit?
questions.explanation: Demand implies MR = 100−4Q. Equating this with 20+0.5Q gives Q ≈ 17.78; demand then gives P ≈ €64.44. The closest pair is Q≈18, P≈€64.
questions.source: Original question Q16; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [Q17] Two supermarket chains repeatedly compete in a small town. Each has an incentive to discount if the rival maintains its price, but both would earn more if neither discounted. Which explanation is strongest?

options.text: Monopolistic competition: strategic interaction is impossible.
Natural monopoly: one firm must have falling average cost at every output.
Perfect competition: each chain is necessarily a price taker.
An oligopoly prisoner’s dilemma: individually attractive discounting can leave both worse off.

questions.explanation: Each chain’s best response depends on its rival. Individually attractive discounting can leave both with lower payoffs, the oligopoly prisoner’s-dilemma mechanism.
questions.source: Original question Q17; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [Q18] A patented pharmaceutical product faces an approaching patent expiry, powerful hospital purchasing groups and a high-cost regulatory approval process for new entrants. Which combination best describes Porter’s forces?

options.text: Buyer power is high; threat of entry is constrained by regulation, while the patent expiry may intensify rivalry or substitutes.
Threat of entry is automatically high because regulation is costly.
Buyer power is necessarily low because hospitals are large.

questions.explanation: Large purchasing groups can exert buyer power. Regulatory approval costs constrain entry, while patent expiry may increase competitive pressure.
questions.source: Original question Q18; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)

questions.stem: [O1] A single-price monopolist faces demand P=100−Q and marginal revenue MR=100−2Q. It has already selected an output of 30 units. Which curve should it use to find the price customers will pay?

options.text: The AC curve at Q=30, regardless of demand
The vertical axis, without reference to output

questions.explanation: For a selected output, price is read from demand/average revenue. At Q=30, P=100−30=70; marginal revenue is not the selling price.
questions.source: Original question O1; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [O2] Relative to an otherwise comparable competitive benchmark, a monopolist restricts output and charges a higher price. Which statement best distinguishes a transfer of surplus from deadweight loss?

options.text: Both are simply additional revenue received by the monopolist.
A transfer moves surplus between consumers and the producer; deadweight loss represents gains from trades that no longer occur.
Deadweight loss is the monopolist's fixed cost; a transfer is its variable cost.
Every euro of consumer-surplus reduction must be destroyed rather than transferred.

questions.explanation: A transfer reallocates surplus between consumers and the producer. Deadweight loss consists of gains from trades that do not occur.
questions.source: Original question O2; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [O3] Why might a government grant patent protection even though the resulting market power can create deadweight loss?

options.text: Patent protection guarantees that the protected firm's price equals marginal cost.
Patent protection removes all research and development costs.
The prospect of protected returns can encourage innovation and drug development, creating a trade-off with restricted output.
Patent protection makes consumer surplus identical to producer surplus.

questions.explanation: Patents can encourage innovation by protecting expected returns, but resulting market power can restrict output and create welfare losses.
questions.source: Original question O3; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [O4] A café operates in a monopolistically competitive market. At its selected output, price exceeds average economic cost. Which method measures its economic profit?

options.text: Multiply the difference between price and average economic cost by quantity sold.

questions.explanation: Economic profit is total revenue less total economic cost: (P−AC)×Q.
questions.source: Original question O4; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [O5] Many differentiated sellers can enter a monopolistically competitive market. Incumbents currently earn positive economic profit. Which sequence best describes the lecture's long-run adjustment?

options.text: Entry reduces each incumbent's demand; equilibrium has demand/AR tangent to AC and zero economic profit.
Entry shifts every incumbent's demand right indefinitely, guaranteeing rising economic profit.
Entry removes differentiation and forces every firm to operate at minimum AC immediately.
Entry stops because positive economic profit is itself a legal barrier.

questions.explanation: Entry attracts customers away from incumbents. Long-run adjustment in this model yields demand/AR tangent to AC and zero economic profit.
questions.source: Original question O5; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [P1] A single-price monopolist faces P=100−Q, MR=100−2Q and constant MC=€20 per unit. Assume it operates and there are no capacity constraints. Using Graph 1 and the equations, which output–price pair maximises profit?
questions.explanation: MR = MC gives 100−2Q=20, so Q=40. Demand gives P=100−40=€60.
questions.source: Original question P1; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [P4] A car manufacturer relies on one component producer whose specialised machinery supplies a crucial part. Switching to another supplier would take months, and withholding the component could halt car production. From the car manufacturer's perspective, which force is most directly illustrated?

options.text: Threat of substitute products bought by motorists

questions.explanation: A crucial specialised input, high switching costs and the risk of withheld supply strengthen supplier bargaining power.
questions.source: Original question P4; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [P5] Three large firms account for most sales in a market. Their products are differentiated and entry is difficult. Before cutting its price, each firm considers whether the other two will match the cut. Which market structure and feature best fit the scenario?

options.text: Perfect competition; each firm faces horizontal demand and can ignore rivals
Monopoly; a single seller faces no existing rivals
Monopolistic competition; many small sellers face easy entry

questions.explanation: A few dominant firms, barriers and attention to rivals’ likely responses identify strategically interdependent oligopoly.
questions.source: Original question P5; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12

questions.stem: [OS17] An electrical utility serves demand at lower average cost as one large provider than as several smaller providers. Splitting it into four equal firms removes these scale economies. Holding other conditions constant, which concern follows?

options.text: Average costs may rise, so creating more firms does not by itself guarantee lower prices.
Average costs must fall because there are more firms.
The industry automatically becomes perfectly competitive.
The change removes all fixed infrastructure costs.

questions.explanation: Losing scale economies may raise average costs. Creating several firms does not by itself ensure lower costs or prices.
questions.source: Original question OS17; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12; OpenStax adaptation: https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/9-self-check-questions

questions.stem: [OS18] Firms A and B each choose simultaneously between keeping a collusive output limit (“collude”) and selling extra output (“cheat”). This is a one-shot game with no later punishment or reward. Each firm seeks the highest payoff for itself. The table lists payoffs as (A’s payoff, B’s payoff), in the same monetary units throughout. A Nash equilibrium is a pair of choices in which neither firm can improve its own payoff by changing its choice alone. Which option lists all pure-strategy Nash equilibria?

options.text: Both collude is the only pure-strategy equilibrium
Both cheat is the only pure-strategy equilibrium
A colludes while B cheats, and A cheats while B colludes
A colludes while B cheats is the only pure-strategy equilibrium

questions.explanation: If B colludes, A prefers cheating (1,050>1,000); if B cheats, A prefers colluding (800>500). If A colludes, B prefers cheating (200>100); if A cheats, B prefers colluding (50>20). Thus (A colludes, B cheats) and (A cheats, B colludes) are both pure-strategy Nash equilibria.
questions.source: Original question OS18; Market Structure lecture slides; Lectures #9–12; OpenStax adaptation: https://openstax.org/books/principles-economics-3e/pages/10-self-check-questions

chapters.title: Absolute & Comparative Advantage
chapters.description: PPFs, opportunity costs, specialisation, terms of trade and consumption gains; trade calculations are optional understanding practice.

questions.stem: [127] Ricardo’s example used cloth and wine. Suppose Ireland can produce 60 barrels of whiskey or 30 cases of wine, while Portugal can produce 20 barrels of whiskey or 20 cases of wine with equal resources. Which country has comparative advantage in wine?

options.text: Portugal, because a case of wine costs 1 barrel of whiskey there, versus 2 in Ireland.
Ireland, because it can produce more whiskey.
Ireland, because it can produce more wine.
Neither, because both can produce wine.

questions.explanation: Wine costs Portugal 20/20 = 1 barrel of whiskey, compared with Ireland’s 60/30 = 2. Portugal has the lower opportunity cost.
questions.source: Original question 127; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [128] Ireland can produce 60 barrels of whiskey or 30 cases of wine with equal resources. What is Ireland’s opportunity cost of one barrel of whiskey?
questions.explanation: Ireland gives up 30 cases of wine to make 60 barrels of whiskey: 30/60 = 0.5 case per barrel.
questions.source: Original question 128; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [129] A simplified example: Micheál Martin can earn €120 per hour doing professional work and mow his lawn in 1 hour. A teenager can earn €15 per hour and mow the lawn in 2 hours. Ignoring other considerations, why might Martin hire the teenager?

options.text: Because Martin has an absolute advantage at mowing.
Because the teenager has a lower monetary opportunity cost of mowing the lawn.
Because teenagers always have a comparative advantage in manual work.
Because Martin cannot mow his lawn.

questions.explanation: Martin forgoes €120; the teenager forgoes 2 × €15 = €30. There is room for a mutually beneficial payment between those costs.
questions.source: Original question 129; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [130] An AI system completes 40 routine reconciliations or 10 complex client-review tasks per hour. An accountant completes 8 reconciliations or 4 reviews. Who has comparative advantage in complex reviews?

options.text: AI, because it completes more reviews per hour.
Neither, because AI is faster at both tasks.
The accountant, because each review costs 2 reconciliations rather than 4 for AI.

questions.explanation: The accountant forgoes 8/4 = 2 reconciliations per review; AI forgoes 40/10 = 4.
questions.source: Original question 130; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [131] An Irish BIS graduate can build 6 dashboards or test 12 security configurations per day. A specialist can build 8 dashboards or test 32 configurations. Who has comparative advantage in dashboards?

options.text: The specialist, because they build more dashboards.
The BIS graduate, because a dashboard costs 2 security tests rather than 4.

questions.explanation: The graduate forgoes 12/6 = 2 security tests per dashboard; the specialist forgoes 32/8 = 4.
questions.source: Original question 131; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [132] Two accounting firms specialise according to comparative advantage and trade services. Which outcome is consistent with the PPF model?

options.text: Both firms must consume exactly on their own PPFs.
Trade can allow each firm to access a service bundle beyond its own production PPF.
Trade shifts each firm’s PPF outward automatically.

questions.explanation: Specialisation and exchange can expand consumption possibilities beyond an individual production frontier without automatically shifting that frontier.
questions.source: Original question 132; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [133] Ireland gives up 2 units of food to produce one software service; Portugal gives up 4. At what trading price (food per software) could both gain?

options.text: Exactly 4 food per software is the only possible price.

questions.explanation: A price strictly between the opportunity costs of 2 and 4 food units permits gains for both; 3 qualifies.
questions.source: Original question 133; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [134] A tariff raises the price of imported accounting software in Ireland. In a standard competitive trade model, what is the most likely effect?

options.text: Irish consumers gain and there is no efficiency loss.
The tariff eliminates the opportunity cost of domestic software.
Some domestic producers may gain, but users pay more and overall efficiency may fall.

questions.explanation: Protection can benefit domestic producers, while higher import prices harm users and distort efficient production and consumption.
questions.source: Original question 134; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [135] A country has comparative advantage in exporting data-processing services. A new foreign tariff makes these exports less competitive. Which conclusion is best?

options.text: Comparative advantage guarantees exports cannot fall.
Trade policy can reduce realised gains from trade even if underlying opportunity costs are unchanged.
The tariff must improve world efficiency.
The exporting country immediately loses all productive ability.

questions.explanation: Tariffs alter market access and trading incentives even when relative productive opportunity costs remain unchanged.
questions.source: Original question 135; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [136] A GenAI platform is faster than a junior accountant at every task. Which statement is most defensible?

options.text: The accountant must be redundant under Ricardo’s theory.
The AI must have comparative advantage in every task.
The accountant may still have comparative advantage in some tasks, but this does not guarantee employment or wages.
Comparative advantage means technology never displaces workers.

questions.explanation: Absolute advantage at every task does not imply comparative advantage at every task. The model alone does not guarantee jobs or wages.
questions.source: Original question 136; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [137] Ireland can produce at most 16 software units or 40 food units; Portugal can produce at most 8 software units or 32 food units, using the same amount of labour. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Ireland has an absolute advantage in both goods, but Portugal has a comparative advantage in food.
Portugal has an absolute advantage in food.
Ireland has a comparative advantage in both goods.
Neither country can gain from trade.

questions.explanation: Ireland produces more of both goods. Food costs Portugal 8/32 = 0.25 software, versus Ireland’s 16/40 = 0.4.
questions.source: Original question 137; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [138] Ireland’s PPF endpoints are 16 software and 40 food. It initially produces and consumes 10 software and 15 food. After specialisation and trade, it consumes 11 software and 18 food. Relative to self-sufficiency, how does Ireland’s consumption change?
questions.explanation: Software rises from 10 to 11, and food from 15 to 18: gains of 1 and 3 respectively.
questions.source: Original question 138; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [139] Ireland specialises in 16 software units and Portugal in 32 food units. Ireland exports 5 software units to Portugal in return for 18 food units. What can Portugal consume after trade?
questions.explanation: Portugal receives 5 software and retains 32 − 18 = 14 food.
questions.source: Original question 139; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [140] In one hour GenAI can produce 20 routine drafts or 4 judgement cases. A human can produce 5 routine drafts or 2 judgement cases. Which statement about comparative advantage is correct?

options.text: GenAI has comparative advantage in both tasks because it has absolute advantage in both.
The human has comparative advantage in judgement cases, although GenAI has absolute advantage in both tasks.
The human has comparative advantage in routine drafts.
Both have the same opportunity cost of a judgement case.

questions.explanation: A human judgement case costs 5/2 = 2.5 drafts; GenAI’s costs 20/4 = 5 drafts. The human has the lower opportunity cost.
questions.source: Original question 140; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [141] Ireland initially consumes (10 software, 15 food). It specialises in 16 software and trades 5 software for 18 food. Suppose an import tariff reduces the food it actually receives by 4 units, with the same software export. Which outcome is correct?

options.text: Ireland consumes (11 software, 14 food), so the new bundle is not better in both goods than self-sufficiency.
Ireland consumes (10 software, 19 food), so it gains food without losing software.
Ireland consumes (11 software, 18 food), so the tariff has no effect.
Ireland consumes (16 software, 14 food), so both goods rise.

questions.explanation: Ireland retains 16 − 5 = 11 software and receives 18 − 4 = 14 food. Compared with (10,15), software rises but food falls; welfare cannot be ranked without preferences.
questions.source: Original question 141; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [T1] Which comparison establishes comparative advantage?

options.text: The largest possible output, regardless of resources
The lowest monetary selling price in every market
The lowest opportunity cost of producing the good
The largest output of both goods simultaneously

questions.explanation: Comparative advantage is identified by the lower opportunity cost, not the larger absolute output.
questions.source: Original question T1; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [T2] With fixed resources and technology, what does a point on a straight-line production possibilities frontier represent?

options.text: A productively efficient feasible output combination
An inefficient combination with unused productive capacity
A combination unattainable through domestic production
A requirement to produce only one good

questions.explanation: A point on the PPF is feasible and productively efficient with the stated resources and technology.
questions.source: Original question T2; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [T3] A country trades and consumes a bundle outside its unchanged domestic PPF. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Trade has automatically shifted its domestic PPF outwards
It must now produce beyond the domestic PPF
Both countries must have specialised completely
Exchange can expand consumption possibilities without expanding domestic production possibilities

questions.explanation: Trade can expand consumption possibilities without shifting the domestic PPF or enabling production outside it.
questions.source: Original question T3; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14

questions.stem: [T4] With equal labour resources and straight-line PPFs, Ireland can make 32 software or 80 food; Portugal can make 16 software or 64 food. What are their opportunity costs of one software unit, respectively?
questions.explanation: One software unit costs Ireland 80/32 = 2.5 food and Portugal 64/16 = 4 food.
questions.source: Original question T4; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14; optional trade-calculation practice, not confirmed test emphasis

questions.stem: [T5] Ireland's straight-line PPF has endpoints of 32 software and 80 food. If it produces 28 software efficiently, how much food can it also produce?
questions.explanation: The frontier is F = 80−2.5S. At S = 28, F = 10.
questions.source: Original question T5; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14; optional trade-calculation practice, not confirmed test emphasis

questions.stem: [T6] Ireland produces (28 software, 10 food) and Portugal produces (0 software, 64 food). Ireland sends 10 software to Portugal in exchange for 31 food. Which pair of post-trade consumption bundles is correct?
questions.explanation: Ireland consumes (28−10, 10+31) = (18,41). Portugal consumes (0+10, 64−31) = (10,33).
questions.source: Original question T6; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14; optional trade-calculation practice, not confirmed test emphasis

questions.stem: [T7] Before specialisation, Ireland produces (16 software,40 food) and Portugal (8 software,32 food). Afterwards, Ireland produces (28 software,10 food) and Portugal (0 software,64 food). How does combined output change?
questions.explanation: Initial combined output is (24,72); afterwards it is (28,74). The change is +4 software and +2 food.
questions.source: Original question T7; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14; optional trade-calculation practice, not confirmed test emphasis

questions.stem: [T8] Ireland's opportunity cost is 2.5 food per software; Portugal's is 4 food per software. They exchange 10 software for 31 food. What is the exchange rate, and does it lie strictly between their opportunity costs?
questions.explanation: The exchange rate is 31/10 = 3.1 food per software, strictly between 2.5 and 4.
questions.source: Original question T8; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14; optional trade-calculation practice, not confirmed test emphasis

questions.stem: [T9] Ireland's straight-line PPF has endpoints of 32 software or 80 food. What is its maximum domestic food production at 18 software, compared with consumption of 41 food after trade?

options.text: 35 food domestically; 41 food is beyond its domestic production frontier at that software quantity
45 food domestically; 41 food is inside its frontier at that software quantity
62 food domestically; 41 food is inside its frontier at that software quantity
41 food domestically; the consumption point must be on its frontier

questions.explanation: At 18 software, domestic food production can reach 80−2.5(18) = 35. Consumption of 41 food is beyond that domestic production frontier.
questions.source: Original question T9; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14; optional trade-calculation practice, not confirmed test emphasis

questions.stem: [T10] With equal resources, the US can produce 500 planes or 1,000 tons of shoes; China can produce 100 planes or 800 tons of shoes. Assuming straight-line PPFs, what are their opportunity costs of one plane and which has comparative advantage in planes?
questions.explanation: A plane costs the US 1,000/500 = 2 tons of shoes and China 800/100 = 8. The US has the lower opportunity cost.
questions.source: Original question T10; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14; optional trade-calculation practice, not confirmed test emphasis

questions.stem: [Q20] A human analyst can complete 6 routine reconciliations or 3 client reviews per day; an AI system can complete 30 reconciliations or 5 reviews per day. Assume comparable output and one day each. Which allocation follows comparative advantage?

options.text: AI specialises in reviews because 5 exceeds 3.
There can be no gains from specialisation when AI is absolutely better at both.
Human specialises in reconciliations because 6 is fewer than 30.
AI specialises in reconciliations; human in reviews, despite AI’s absolute advantage in both.

questions.explanation: One review costs the human 6/3 = 2 reconciliations and AI 30/5 = 6. Humans have comparative advantage in reviews and AI in reconciliations.
questions.source: Original question Q20; Absolute and Comparative Advantage lecture slides; Lecture #14; supplied Sample+2204+MCQ.docx (answer derived from stated data; no official key supplied)
